etymology: Hebrew Achor, "trouble"; the valley where Achan was judged, which God promised to make "a door of hope."
biblical_def: The valley of Achor, whose name means "trouble," was the place where Achan and his household were stoned after his sin had brought defeat upon Israel at Ai. Achan had taken of the accursed thing from Jericho, and for his hidden theft the army was routed; when the sin was uncovered, Joshua said, "Why hast thou troubled us? the LORD shall trouble thee this day. And all Israel stoned him with stones... Wherefore the name of that place was called, The valley of Achor, unto this day" (Josh 7:25-26). It was a place of judgment, where sin in the camp was purged. Yet the prophets transformed its meaning into one of the Bible's most beautiful promises of grace. Through Hosea the LORD pledged to His wayward people, "I will give her... the valley of Achor for a door of hope" (Hos 2:15), and Isaiah foresaw it as a resting-place for the flock (Isa 65:10). The valley of trouble would become a doorway into hope. Achor stands in the dictionary as the place where trouble is turned to hope, a witness that sin must be judged, yet that the God of grace can make the very valley of our trouble — rightly judged and repented of — the door through which we enter into renewed fellowship and hope.

corruption_paragraphs: Sin-tolerated correction. Israel could not stand before its enemies while the accursed thing was hidden in the camp. The valley of Achor teaches that hidden sin brings defeat, and must be uncovered and judged before blessing returns. The dictionary holds the seriousness of sin in the church: it cannot be tolerated or concealed without cost, and the path to renewed strength runs through honest confession and the purging of evil from among the people of God.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the gospel turn from trouble to hope. The God who judged sin at Achor promised to make that very valley "a door of hope" (Hos 2:15). The dictionary commends this grace: when sin is judged and repented of, God can transform the place of our deepest trouble into the doorway of renewed fellowship and song, so that the valley named for trouble becomes the threshold of hope for those who seek Him.

etymology: Hebrew Baca, "weeping" (or a balsam tree of dry places); the valley of weeping that the pilgrim turns into a well of springs.
biblical_def: The valley of Baca, meaning "weeping" (or named for balsam trees that grow in arid ground), appears in the great pilgrim psalm as an image of the hard and sorrowful places through which the people of God pass on their way to Zion. "Blessed is the man whose strength is in thee; in whose heart are the ways of them. Who passing through the valley of Baca make it a well; the rain also filleth the pools" (Psa 84:5-6). The pilgrims, set on going up to the house of God, do not avoid the valley of weeping but pass through it — and as they go, they make it a well, turning the place of tears into a source of refreshment, while the rain of heaven fills the pools. "They go from strength to strength, every one of them in Zion appeareth before God" (Psa 84:7). The valley of Baca stands in the dictionary as the valley of weeping made a well, a picture of the believer's pilgrimage through sorrow: those whose strength is in God do not merely endure the hard places but transform them, digging wells of refreshment in the desert of grief, and going from strength to strength until they appear before God in Zion.
webster_summary: The "valley of weeping" in Psalm 84:6 that pilgrims, whose strength is in God, turn into a well of springs as they journey to Zion; a picture of transforming sorrow into refreshment on the way to God.

corruption_paragraphs: Sorrow-avoided correction. The natural heart seeks a path to God that skirts all weeping. The pilgrim psalm assumes the valley of Baca lies on the road to Zion, and blesses those who pass through it. The dictionary holds that the way to glory runs through tribulation (Acts 14:22); the believer is not promised exemption from the valley of weeping but the strength to pass through it, and even to make it a well of refreshment for himself and others.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the transformation of sorrow by faith. Those whose strength is in God do not merely endure the valley of weeping; they make it a well, and heaven's rain fills the pools. The dictionary commends this hope: the believer's light affliction works a far more exceeding weight of glory (2 Cor 4:17), and faith digs wells in the desert of grief, going from strength to strength until it appears before God in Zion.

etymology: Hebrew Yehoshaphat, "the LORD judges"; the valley where God declares He will gather and judge the nations.
biblical_def: The valley of Jehoshaphat, whose name means "the LORD judges," is named in the prophecy of Joel as the place of God's final judgment upon the nations. "I will also gather all nations, and will bring them down into the valley of Jehoshaphat, and will plead with them there for my people and for my heritage Israel, whom they have scattered among the nations" (Joel 3:2). There the LORD summons the nations to account for their treatment of His people, and there He sits in judgment: "Let the heathen be wakened, and come up to the valley of Jehoshaphat: for there will I sit to judge all the heathen round about" (Joel 3:12). The same scene is called "the valley of decision," for "the day of the LORD is near in the valley of decision" (Joel 3:14). Whether the name marks a literal place or stands symbolically for the certainty of God's judgment, its meaning is plain: the LORD will judge the nations. The valley of Jehoshaphat stands in the dictionary as the valley of the LORD's judgment, a solemn witness that history moves toward a reckoning in which God will vindicate His people, judge the nations for their deeds, and prove Himself the righteous Judge whose very name this valley bears.
webster_summary: The valley ("the LORD judges") where God declares He will gather and judge the nations (Joel 3:2, 12), also called "the valley of decision"; a witness that history moves toward God's righteous reckoning with the nations.

corruption_summary: Jehoshaphat is corrupted when the final judgment of the nations is denied or spiritualized away; its lesson is that God will surely judge the nations in righteousness, vindicating His people.
corruption_paragraphs: Judgment-denied correction. A sentimental age denies any final reckoning, imagining a God who never judges. The valley of Jehoshaphat — "the LORD judges" — declares the opposite: God has appointed a day in which He will judge the world in righteousness (Acts 17:31). The dictionary holds the certainty of final judgment, including the judgment of the nations for their deeds; a God who would not judge evil would be neither just nor a comfort to the oppressed who cry for vindication.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the comfort of God's judgment to His suffering people. The LORD gathers the nations to "plead... for my people" whom they have scattered and oppressed. The dictionary commends this hope: the people of God, often wronged and seemingly without recourse, may entrust their cause to the righteous Judge, who will at last set all accounts right in the valley where the LORD judges, and vindicate His heritage before all the nations.

etymology: Hebrew Ge-Hinnom, "valley of Hinnom"; a ravine south of Jerusalem defiled by child sacrifice, the source of the New Testament word for hell, Gehenna.
biblical_def: The valley of Hinnom (Ge-Hinnom) was a ravine south of Jerusalem with a dark and dreadful history, which gave its name to the New Testament word for hell. There, at a place called Topheth, apostate Israelites under wicked kings like Ahaz and Manasseh burned their children in the fire as sacrifices to the false god Molech — an abomination the LORD said never entered into His heart to command (Jer 7:31). "Moreover he caused his children to pass through the fire in the valley of the son of Hinnom" (2 Chr 33:6). The godly king Josiah "defiled Topheth, which is in the valley of the children of Hinnom, that no man might make his son or his daughter to pass through the fire to Molech" (2 Kgs 23:10). Because of its defilement and its association with fire and judgment, the valley became an image of the place of final punishment; the Greek Gehenna, drawn from Ge-Hinnom, is the word the Lord Jesus most often used for hell (Matt 5:22; 10:28; 23:33). The valley of Hinnom stands in the dictionary as the place of abominable idolatry that became the very emblem of hell, a witness both to the horror of forsaking God for false gods and to the reality of the eternal judgment its name came to signify.
webster_summary: A ravine south of Jerusalem (Ge-Hinnom) where apostate Israel burned children to Molech, defiled by Josiah; its name became the Greek Gehenna, the word the Lord Jesus most often used for hell.

corruption_summary: Hinnom is corrupted when the reality of hell its name signifies is denied, and its lesson dismissed; it witnesses both to the horror of idolatry and the shedding of innocent blood, and to the certainty of eternal judgment.
corruption_paragraphs: Hell-denied correction. Modern sentiment recoils from the doctrine of hell, the very reality the Lord Jesus signified by the word drawn from this valley. He warned plainly of Gehenna, "the fire that never shall be quenched" (Mark 9:43), and bade men fear Him able to destroy both soul and body in hell (Matt 10:28). The dictionary holds the reality of eternal judgment that Hinnom's name came to bear; to deny hell is to contradict the Savior, who spoke of it more than any other, and out of love warned sinners to flee it.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition beyond this. The principle to recover is the horror of forsaking God for idols and the shedding of innocent blood. In Hinnom, apostate Israel burned its own children to a false god — a crime that joined idolatry to the slaughter of the innocent. The dictionary holds, with abiding application, the sanctity of the lives of children and the abomination of shedding innocent blood in the service of false gods; Hinnom warns every age against the idols that demand the sacrifice of the defenseless.

etymology: Hebrew Massah, "testing," and Meribah, "strife"; the place at Rephidim where Israel tempted the LORD and Moses struck the rock.
biblical_def: Massah ("testing") and Meribah ("strife") were the twin names given to the place at Rephidim where Israel, lacking water, quarreled with Moses and put the LORD to the test. "And he called the name of the place Massah, and Meribah, because of the chiding of the children of Israel, and because they tempted the LORD, saying, Is the LORD among us, or not?" (Exo 17:7). At the LORD's command Moses struck the rock in Horeb, and water came out for the people to drink (Exo 17:6). The sin was grievous: having seen the plagues, the Red Sea, the manna, and the cloud, Israel still doubted God's presence and demanded proof. Scripture treats Massah and Meribah as a lasting warning against unbelief and the testing of God: "Harden not your heart, as in the provocation, and as in the day of temptation in the wilderness: when your fathers tempted me, proved me, and saw my work" (Psa 95:8-9), a text the Epistle to the Hebrews applies to the church (Heb 3:8). Massah and Meribah stand in the dictionary as the place of Israel's provocation, a solemn warning that to doubt God's presence and goodness after all His proven mercies is to harden the heart and tempt the LORD, and a call to believe and trust Him in the dry places rather than to chide and test Him.
webster_summary: The place at Rephidim ("testing" and "strife") where Israel, lacking water, tempted the LORD asking "Is the LORD among us, or not?" (Exo 17:7); a lasting warning against unbelief and hardening the heart (Psa 95:8; Heb 3:8).

corruption_summary: Massah and Meribah need no defense from redefinition; their lesson is the sin of tempting God and hardening the heart in unbelief despite His proven mercies.
corruption_paragraphs: Unbelief-excused correction. The natural heart, meeting hardship, doubts God's presence and demands fresh proof, as Israel did asking, "Is the LORD among us, or not?" Scripture names this tempting of God a grievous sin, committed by a people who had already seen His mighty works. The dictionary holds that to distrust God's goodness and presence after all His proven mercies is unbelief, not honest doubt; the believer is called to trust the God who has shown Himself faithful, even in the dry places where no water yet appears.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the warning against hardening the heart. The Holy Spirit, through the Psalm and the Epistle to the Hebrews, holds up Massah and Meribah to the church: "Harden not your hearts, as in the provocation" (Heb 3:8). The dictionary commends this solemn application: persistent unbelief hardens the heart and provokes the LORD, and the people of God in every age must hear His voice today, believe His promises, and not repeat the provocation of the wilderness.

etymology: A desert region between Elim and Sinai where God first gave Israel manna; the name is a place-name (Hebrew Sin), unrelated to the English word for sin.
biblical_def: The wilderness of Sin was a desert region that Israel entered between Elim and Mount Sinai, about a month and a half after leaving Egypt, where the LORD began to feed them with manna from heaven. (The name Sin is a Hebrew place-name, having nothing to do with the English word "sin.") There the whole congregation murmured against Moses and Aaron, complaining that they had been brought into the wilderness to die of hunger, and looking back wistfully to the fleshpots of Egypt (Exo 16:2-3). The LORD answered their murmuring not with judgment but with provision: "Behold, I will rain bread from heaven for you" (Exo 16:4). Each morning the manna fell, and at evening the quails came up; the people gathered the manna daily, a double portion before the Sabbath, learning to depend on God for their bread one day at a time. This manna, the "bread from heaven," the Lord Jesus would later declare a type of Himself, the true bread that gives life to the world (John 6:31-35). The wilderness of Sin stands in the dictionary as the place where God first gave the manna, a witness to His faithful provision in answer even to murmuring, and a foreshadowing of Christ, the bread of life, on whom His people are taught to feed daily by faith.
webster_summary: A desert between Elim and Sinai (Exo 16) where God first gave Israel manna in answer to their murmuring; a type of Christ, the true bread from heaven. The name is a Hebrew place-name, unrelated to the English word "sin."

corruption_paragraphs: Provision-doubted correction. Israel doubted that God could feed them and longed for Egypt's fleshpots. The LORD answered their murmuring with grace, raining bread from heaven. The dictionary holds the lesson of daily dependence: God gives His people their bread one day at a time, teaching them to trust Him for each day's need rather than to hoard or to fear, as the Lord taught us to pray, "Give us this day our daily bread."

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the manna as a type of Christ. The Lord Jesus declared that the manna pointed to Himself: "my Father giveth you the true bread from heaven" (John 6:32), and "I am the bread of life." The dictionary commends this fulfillment: as Israel fed daily on the manna in the wilderness, so the believer feeds daily by faith on Christ, the living bread come down from heaven, who alone sustains the soul on its pilgrimage to the promised land.

etymology: Hebrew Paran; a large wilderness south of Canaan from which the twelve spies were sent into the promised land.
biblical_def: The wilderness of Paran was a large desert region south of Canaan, in the Sinai peninsula, where Israel encamped during the wilderness years and from which the twelve spies were sent to search out the promised land. After leaving Sinai, "the children of Israel took their journeys... and the cloud rested in the wilderness of Paran" (Num 10:12). From Paran, at Kadesh, "Moses by the commandment of the LORD sent" the twelve men to spy out Canaan (Num 13:3, 26); and it was to Paran they returned with their report, ten of them bringing an evil report that provoked the people's unbelief and the forty years of wandering. Paran had earlier been the dwelling-place of Ishmael, who "dwelt in the wilderness of Paran" after he and Hagar were sent away (Gen 21:21). Long after, David withdrew to the wilderness of Paran at the death of Samuel (1 Sam 25:1). Paran stands in the dictionary as the wilderness of the spies and of unbelief, the place from which Israel looked into the land of promise and turned back in fear, a solemn witness that the borders of blessing may be reached and yet forfeited by unbelief, and that the report we believe — the faith of Caleb and Joshua or the fear of the ten — determines whether we enter the rest of God.

corruption_paragraphs: Unbelief-at-the-border correction. From Paran, Israel stood at the very threshold of the promised land, sent the spies, and then turned back in fear at the evil report of the ten. The dictionary holds the sobering lesson of Hebrews: "they could not enter in because of unbelief" (Heb 3:19). It is possible to come near the blessing of God and forfeit it through fear and distrust; the borders of Canaan are reached by many who never enter, because they believe the report of fear rather than the promise of God.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the power of the report we believe. Twelve men saw the same land; two believed God and were ready to go up, ten saw only giants and walled cities. The dictionary commends the faith of Caleb and Joshua: faith reckons with the promise and power of God, not merely with the visible obstacles, and those who believe the good report — that the LORD is able to bring His people in — enter the rest that unbelief forfeits.

They could not enter in because of unbelief (Heb 3:19) — the failure that began at Paran.
Paran witnesses that the borders of blessing may be forfeited through unbelief.

etymology: Hebrew Tsin; a desert on the southern border of Canaan, the site of Kadesh, Miriam's death, and the waters of Meribah-Kadesh.
biblical_def: The wilderness of Zin was a desert region on the southern border of the promised land, distinct from the wilderness of Sin, and the scene of several weighty events near the end of Israel's wandering. It contained Kadesh, where the congregation came in the first month, "and Miriam died there, and was buried there" (Num 20:1). There, when the people again had no water and chided with Moses, the LORD told him to speak to the rock; but Moses, provoked, struck it twice and said, "Hear now, ye rebels; must we fetch you water out of this rock?" (Num 20:10). Water came, but because Moses and Aaron had not sanctified the LORD in the eyes of Israel, the LORD told them they would not bring the congregation into the land (Num 20:12); these were "the waters of Meribah in Kadesh in the wilderness of Zin" (Num 27:14). The wilderness of Zin also marked the southern boundary of Canaan in the allotment of the land (Num 34:3). Zin stands in the dictionary as the wilderness of Meribah-Kadesh, where even Moses failed at the rock and was barred from the land, a solemn witness that God will be sanctified by those who draw near Him, that leaders are held to account, and that one act of unbelief and disobedience, even in a faithful servant, bears real consequence before a holy God.
webster_summary: A desert on Canaan's southern border (distinct from the wilderness of Sin); the site of Kadesh, Miriam's death, and the waters of Meribah, where Moses struck the rock and was barred from the promised land (Num 20).
webster_full: WILDERNESS OF ZIN, proper noun. A desert on the southern border of Canaan.
Distinct from the wilderness of Sin; the site of Kadesh.
Where Miriam died and was buried (Num 20:1).
Where Moses struck the rock instead of speaking to it (Num 20:10-11).
Where the waters of Meribah cost Moses and Aaron entrance to the land (Num 20:12; 27:14).
scriptures: Num 20:1
Then came the children of Israel, even the whole congregation, into the desert of Zin in the first month: and the people abode in Kadesh; and Miriam died there, and was buried there.
And Moses and Aaron gathered the congregation together before the rock, and he said unto them, Hear now, ye rebels; must we fetch you water out of this rock?

And the LORD spake unto Moses and Aaron, Because ye believed me not, to sanctify me in the eyes of the children of Israel, therefore ye shall not bring this congregation into the land which I have given them.
...that is the water of Meribah in Kadesh in the wilderness of Zin.
corruption_summary: Zin needs no defense from redefinition; its lesson is that God will be sanctified by those who draw near Him, and that even a faithful leader's act of unbelief and disobedience bears real consequence.
corruption_paragraphs: Consequence-denied correction. A casual view of sin assumes that a faithful servant's lapse carries no real weight. The wilderness of Zin teaches otherwise: Moses, the meekest of men and the LORD's faithful servant, struck the rock in anger and was barred from the land he had labored forty years to reach. The dictionary holds that God will be sanctified by those who come near Him (Lev 10:3); leaders especially are held to account, and one act of unbelief, even in a great servant, has real and lasting consequence before a holy God.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the holiness of God in the conduct of His servants. The LORD's charge was that Moses and Aaron "believed me not, to sanctify me in the eyes of the children of Israel" (Num 20:12). The dictionary commends the sober lesson: those who lead and speak for God bear a heavy responsibility to represent Him truly, and the failure to honor His holiness before the people is no small thing, even when the water still flows.
roots_summary: A desert on Canaan's southern border (distinct from the wilderness of Sin); the site of Kadesh, Miriam's death, and the waters of Meribah, where Moses was barred from the land.

etymology: Hebrew Shur, "wall"; a wilderness east of Egypt where Hagar met the Angel of the LORD and where Israel journeyed after the Red Sea.
biblical_def: The wilderness of Shur was a desert region on the northeastern border of Egypt, the scene of two significant encounters. First, it was here that Hagar, fleeing from Sarai, was found by the Angel of the LORD "by a fountain of water in the wilderness... by the fountain in the way to Shur" (Gen 16:7). The Angel comforted and counseled her, promised to multiply her seed, and she called the name of the LORD that spoke to her, "Thou God seest me" (Gen 16:13) — one of the great revelations of the God who sees the afflicted and forsaken. Second, the wilderness of Shur was the first region Israel entered after crossing the Red Sea: "So Moses brought Israel from the Red sea, and they went out into the wilderness of Shur; and they went three days in the wilderness, and found no water" (Exo 15:22) — a journey that brought them to the bitter waters of Marah. Shur stands in the dictionary as the wilderness where the God who sees met a fleeing slave-woman, and where redeemed Israel first walked after the great deliverance, a witness that the LORD sees and meets the afflicted in their wilderness, that no forsaken soul is beyond His notice, and that even the dry beginning of the redeemed life is under the eye of the God who provides.
webster_summary: A wilderness east of Egypt where the Angel of the LORD found the fleeing Hagar, who called Him "Thou God seest me" (Gen 16:7-13), and the first region Israel entered after the Red Sea (Exo 15:22); a witness to the God who sees the afflicted.
webster_full: WILDERNESS OF SHUR, proper noun. "Wall"; a desert east of Egypt.
Where the Angel of the LORD found the fleeing Hagar by a fountain (Gen 16:7).
Where Hagar called the LORD "Thou God seest me" (Gen 16:13).
The first region Israel entered after crossing the Red Sea (Exo 15:22).
Where Israel went three days and found no water, coming to Marah.
scriptures: Gen 16:7
And the angel of the LORD found her by a fountain of water in the wilderness, by the fountain in the way to Shur.
And she called the name of the LORD that spake unto her, Thou God seest me: for she said, Have I also here looked after him that seeth me?
So Moses brought Israel from the Red sea, and they went out into the wilderness of Shur; and they went three days in the wilderness, and found no water.
Whither shall I go from thy spirit? or whither shall I flee from thy presence?
corruption_summary: Shur needs no defense from redefinition; its lesson is that the God who sees meets the afflicted and forsaken in their wilderness, and watches over the dry beginnings of the redeemed life.
corruption_paragraphs: Forgotten-by-God correction. The afflicted often feel unseen and forsaken, as Hagar did, fleeing alone into the desert. Yet the Angel of the LORD found her, and she learned that He is "the God that seeth." The dictionary holds this comfort: there is no wilderness so remote, no soul so forsaken, that the eye of God does not reach it; He sees the affliction of the despised and the runaway, meets them in their distress, and is not far from any one of them (Psa 139:7).

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is God's care over the dry beginnings of the redeemed life. Israel's first steps after the Red Sea led into the waterless wilderness of Shur. The dictionary commends the lesson: redemption is not the end of trial but the beginning of a pilgrimage that often passes through dry and difficult places. Yet the same God who sees Hagar watches over His redeemed people, and the wilderness journey, however thirsty its start, is under the eye and care of the God who provides.
roots_summary: A wilderness east of Egypt where the Angel of the LORD found the fleeing Hagar (Gen 16:7-13) and the first region Israel entered after the Red Sea (Exo 15:22); a witness to the God who sees.

etymology: Hebrew Siddim; a valley near the Salt Sea, full of slimepits, the site of the battle of the kings and Lot's capture.
biblical_def: The valley of Siddim was a region near the Salt (Dead) Sea, "full of slimepits" (bitumen pits), the scene of the battle of the kings in the days of Abram. When the five kings of the plain, including the kings of Sodom and Gomorrah, rebelled against Chedorlaomer and his allies after years of servitude, the armies met in the valley of Siddim (Gen 14:3, 8). The kings of Sodom and Gomorrah were defeated and fled, and some "fell there" into the slimepits; the victorious eastern kings carried off the goods of Sodom and Gomorrah — and with them Lot, Abram's nephew, who dwelt in Sodom (Gen 14:10-12). When word reached Abram, he armed his trained servants, pursued the kings far to the north, defeated them by night, and brought back Lot and all the people and goods (Gen 14:14-16). Returning, he was met by Melchizedek, king of Salem and priest of the most high God, and gave him tithes of all. The valley of Siddim stands in the dictionary as the place of the battle of the kings and Lot's capture, a witness to the peril of pitching one's tent toward Sodom, to the courage of Abram who risked all to rescue his erring kinsman, and to the dignity of faith that, having conquered, refused the spoils of the king of Sodom and honored the priest of the most high God.
webster_summary: A valley near the Salt Sea, full of slimepits (Gen 14:3, 10), where the battle of the kings was fought and Lot was captured; Abram pursued and rescued him, then met Melchizedek. A witness to the peril of Sodom and the courage of faith.

Where the kings of Sodom and Gomorrah were defeated and fled.
Where Lot, dwelling in Sodom, was carried off captive (Gen 14:12).
From which Abram pursued and rescued Lot, then met Melchizedek (Gen 14:14-18).
scriptures: Gen 14:3
All these were joined together in the vale of Siddim, which is the salt sea.
And the vale of Siddim was full of slimepits; and the kings of Sodom and Gomorrah fled, and fell there; and they that remained fled to the mountain.
And they took Lot, Abram's brother's son, who dwelt in Sodom, and his goods, and departed.
And he brought back all the goods, and also brought again his brother Lot, and his goods, and the women also, and the people.
corruption_summary: Siddim needs no defense from redefinition; its lessons are the peril of pitching toward Sodom, the courage of faith that rescues the erring, and the refusal of the world's spoils.
corruption_paragraphs: Worldly-entanglement correction. Lot had pitched his tent toward Sodom and come to dwell in it, and at Siddim he was swept up in its judgment and carried off captive. The dictionary holds the warning: those who entangle themselves with the world for its advantages share its perils; Lot's nearness to Sodom cost him his peace and freedom, and is a standing caution against making one's home in the place of wickedness for the sake of its good land.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the courage and dignity of faith. Abram risked everything to rescue his erring nephew, pursuing a victorious army with a small band, and God gave him the victory; yet he refused the spoils offered by the king of Sodom, that no man might say he had made Abram rich (Gen 14:23), and honored Melchizedek, priest of the most high God. The dictionary commends both: faith rescues the erring at cost to itself, and faith refuses to be enriched by the world it has overcome.
